# FSI Publications Style Sheet - Border Security & Public Safety series - rev. 3 (Jun 2026)
Owner: Vance Tolliver, Director of Publications

## A. Copy
A1. AP style except where noted. Headlines in title case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "illegal alien" (statutory term, 8 U.S.C. 1365) in body copy; "noncitizen" when quoting federal data that uses it.
A3. Lead with public safety and victims. The series argues for stronger interior enforcement; copy should be persuasive, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation
B1. Every figure carries its source and date. Population, timeframe and methodology notes go in the appendix notes, not in body copy, the fact sheet or cards.
B2. Prefer federal primary sources (ICE, USSC, GAO, BJS) over secondary analyses.
B3. Counter-research (e.g. Cato's Texas DPS analyses): appendix only, one line, followed by CIS's methodological critique.
B4. Charts: FSI navy #1F3A5F / red #B22234; y-axis starts at zero.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: Agency/author, Title, Date, URL.
C2. Fact sheet: every stat footnoted.

# Outline - Brief No. 14 (B. Kessler, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: federal data show a serious public-safety cost from illegal immigration and weak interior enforcement; Congress should (1) fund detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, (2) mandate ICE detainer compliance / penalise sanctuary jurisdictions, (3) expand 287(g), (4) require DHS public reporting on releases.
Sections: 1. The non-detained docket. 2. Federal sentencing. 3. State data (Texas). 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Victim stories: Laken Riley (Athens, GA, Feb 2024) is fine to mention briefly; do not invent others.

# Source tables - Brief No. 14 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. ICE non-detained docket - homicide convictions
- 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions on ICE's non-detained docket as of 21 July 2024.
- Source: ICE letter (Patrick J. Lechleitner) to Rep. Tony Gonzales, 25 Sep 2024.
- Context (DHS/ICE statements, Sep-Oct 2024): records go back roughly four decades and cover entries under all administrations; the non-detained docket includes people currently incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities; ICE did not say how many.

## T2. Federal sentencing, FY2024 (U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Non-U.S. Citizen Federal Offenders, FY2024)
- Non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 individuals = 34.7% of all individuals sentenced.
- Primary guideline for noncitizens: immigration 72.3%; drug trafficking 17.6%; other 10.1%.
- 88.7% of noncitizens sentenced were illegal aliens; 8.5% legal aliens.
- GAO-24-107598: number of noncitizens sentenced fell 27% FY2018 -> FY2023.

## T3. Texas DPS conviction data
- Cato Institute (A. Nowrasteh), Texas DPS data 2013-2022: homicide conviction rate per 100,000 - illegal immigrants 2.2, native-born Americans 3.0 (illegal immigrants 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide). Cato also finds lower all-crime arrest/conviction rates; notes data quality caveats for non-homicide offenses.
- Center for Immigration Studies: disputes Cato's denominators (argues Cato misses illegal immigrants identified only after incarceration) and concludes illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates in Texas.

HTTP 200
Federally Sentenced Non-U.S. Citizens | United States Sentencing Commission 

 Skip to main content

 Federally Sentenced Non-U.S. Citizens

 Of the 66,662 cases reported to the Commission in fiscal year 2025, 28,886 involved non-U.S. citizens. 1 Non-U.S. citizens accounted for 44% of all individuals sentenced in fiscal year 2025.
 Click the cover for the PDF handout or learn more below.  
 Individual and Offense Characteristics

 94% of non-U.S. citizens sentenced in the federal system were men.

 95% were Hispanic, 2% were Black, 2% were White, and 2% were Other races.

 Their average age was 37 years. 

 92% were illegal aliens, 6% were legal aliens, 1% were extradited aliens, and 1% were unknown status.

 66% were from Mexico, 10% from Honduras, 8% from Guatemala, 3% from El Salvador, 3% from the Dominican Republic, and 11% originated from other countries.

 The most common guidelines under which non-U.S. citizens were sentenced include: Immigration (79%); Drug Trafficking (12%); Fraud (3%);  Firearms (2%); Money Laundering (1%); and Administration of Justice (1%). 2 

 59% had little or no prior criminal history (Criminal History Category I); 21% were CHC II;
 13% were CHC III;
 4% were CHC IV;
 2% were CHC V;
 1% were CHC VI.

 The top five districts for sentenced non-U.S. citizens were: Western District of Texas (7,346);
 Southern District of Texas (4,814);
 District of Arizona (2,576);
 District of New Mexico (2,150);
 Southern District of California (747).

 The top five districts where sentenced non-U.S. citizens comprised the highest proportion of the overall caseloads were: District of Northern Mariana Islands (82%);
 Western District of Texas (80%);
 District of New Mexico (80%);
 Southern District of Texas (72%);
 District of Arizona (66%).

 Punishment
 The average sentence for non-U.S. citizens was 21 months. 3 

 97% were sentenced to prison.

 9% were convicted of an offense carrying a mandatory minimum penalty.

 Sentences Relative to the Guideline Range
 79% of sentences for non-U.S. citizens were under the Guidelines Manual. 63% were within the guideline range.

 10% were Early Disposition Program (EDP) departures. 4 The average sentence reduction was 44%. 

 3% were substantial assistance departures. The average sentence reduction was 44%. 

 2% were some other downward departure. The average sentence reduction was 42%. 

 Less than 1% were upward departures. The average sentence increase was 106%. 

 21% of sentences for non-U.S. citizens were variances. 15% were downward variances. The average sentence reduction was 39%. 

 6% were upward variances. The average sentence increase was 65%. 

 The average guideline minimum and the average sentence imposed have fluctuated over the past five years. The average guideline minimum was 33 months in fiscal year 2021 and 25 months in fiscal year 2025.

 The average sentence imposed was 25 months in fiscal year 2021 and 21 months in fiscal year 2025.

 1 Cases with incomplete sentencing information were excluded from the analysis.
 2  The most common guidelines under which U.S. citizens were sentenced include: Drug Trafficking (36%); Firearms (21%); Fraud (12%); Immigration (7%); Child Pornography (4%); Sexual Abuse (4%);  and Robbery (3%).
 3  The average sentence for U.S. citizens was 71 months.
 4  “Early Disposition Program" (or EDP) departures are departures where the government sought a sentence below the guideline range because the defendant participated in the government’s Early Disposition Program, through which cases are resolved in an expedited manner. See USSG §5K3.1.

 Delegation of Immigration Authority Section 287(g) Immigration and Nationality Act 

 Delegation of Immigration Authority Section 287(g) Immigration and Nationality Act

 ICE’s 287(g) Program
 The Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 added Section 287(g) to the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), authorizing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to delegate state and local law enforcement officers the authority to perform specified immigration officer functions under ICE’s direction and oversight.
 The Program enhances the safety and security of our nation’s communities by allowing ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) to partner with state, local, and tribal law enforcement agencies to identify and remove criminal aliens who are amenable to removal from the United States.
 ICE recognizes the importance of its relationships with law enforcement partners—including state and local agencies—to carry out its critical mission.
 Through the delegation of specified immigration officer duties, the program allows ICE to enhance collaboration with state and local law enforcement partners to protect the homeland through the arrest and removal of aliens who undermine the safety of our nation’s communities and the integrity of U.S. immigration laws.
 What’s in It for Your Law Enforcement Agency?
 The 287(g) Program benefits state and local law enforcement agencies in several ways — but most notably, it helps you keep your community safe from potentially dangerous criminal aliens. Your law enforcement officers will get access to ICE resources and training. ICE covers the cost of training (see the later section, “287(g) Training Available to State and Local Law Enforcement,” for more information).
 Your agency or office may be eligible for the Department of Justice’s State Criminal Alien Assistance Program . This Department of Justice program administers SCAAP awards and provides federal funding to states and political subdivisions of states, including municipalities that incur costs for incarcerating certain criminal aliens. This is entirely separate from the 287(g) program. 
 ICE 287(g) Program Map

 287(g) Program Models
 ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations operates three 287(g) models:
 The  Jail Enforcement Model allows designated immigration officers to identify and process removable aliens who have pending or active criminal charges.
 The  Task Force Model  enhances public safety and national security by allowing designated immigration officers to enforce limited immigration authority while performing routine police duties or as an active participant in an ICE-led task force.
 The Warrant Service Officer Model allows designated immigration officers to serve and execute administrative warrants on aliens in their custody.
 How Can Your Agency Participate in the ICE 287(g) Program?
 On January 20, 2025, President Donald J. Trump issued Executive Order (EO) 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion . This EO requires ICE to authorize State and local law enforcement officials, as the Secretary of Homeland Security determines are qualified and appropriate, under section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act to the maximum extent permitted by law. Several states, including but not limited to Georgia and Florida, have passed, or are considering, State legislation mandating law enforcement agencies (LEAs) seek out or enter into memorandums of agreement (MOA) with ICE pursuant to a partnership under the 287(g) Program.
 Participation in the 287(g) Program is limited to LEAs only. LEAs interested in participating in the 287(g) Program must sign an MOA with ICE. LEAs will nominate officers to participate in the 287(g) Program. Nominees must possess U.S. citizenship, complete and pass a background investigation, and have knowledge of and have enforced laws and regulations related to law enforcement activities at their jurisdictions. Task Force Model nominees must also have at least two (2) years of total law enforcement officer experience. Nominees will receive training at the expense of ICE related to the immigration duties pertinent to the applicable MOA.
 LEAs interested in becoming a law enforcement partner under the 287(g) Program must submit a signed MOA to ICE at ERO287g@ice.dhs.gov . These forms can be found below.

 Please click on the applicable MOA (fillable), complete and sign in its entirety, and email back to the 287(g) program team at: ERO287g@ice.dhs.gov .

 How Can I Convince My Chief or Sheriff to Participate in 287(g)?
 ICE has several resources, including this page, that can help you show your chief, sheriff or team all the benefits the 287(g) Program provides. From here, you can also download and print ICE’s:
 287(g) fact sheet. 
 287(g) brochure. 
 If you have any questions about participating in the ICE 287(g) program, how to complete the necessary forms, what is required, or would like additional information, please do not hesitate to email ERO287g@ice.dhs.gov ; your inquiry will be promptly answered within one business day.

 As of October 15, 2026 10:58 am ICE has signed 2,679 Memorandums of Agreement for ​287(g) programs covering ​38 states and 2 ​U.S. Territories. ​These include JEM agreements ​with 183 ​law ​enforcement ​agencies ​in ​29 ​states and 1 ​U.S. Territory, 287(g) ​WSO agreements ​with ​572 ​law ​enforcement ​agencies ​in ​34 ​states, and 287(g) TFM ​agreements ​with 1,924 agencies ​in ​32 ​states and 2 ​U.S. Territories.

 ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations Statistics 

 ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations Statistics

 U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) officers enforce immigration laws within the interior to preserve national security and public safety.

 ERO manages all aspects of the immigration enforcement process, including the identification, arrest, detention and removal of aliens who are subject to removal or are unlawfully present in the United States.

 Like all law enforcement agencies, ERO officers prioritize their enforcement actions based on agency and department priorities, funding and capacity. ERO operations are flexible enough to allow its officers to respond to events such as spikes in border crossings, modifications to U.S. laws, pandemics, and natural disasters at home and abroad.

 The following dashboards present for the first time information and trends in arrests, detentions, removals and alternatives to detention as of December 31, 2024. 

 The dashboards will be updated quarterly.

 "With the public release of this enforcement data, ICE is demonstrating its commitment to openness and transparency. We will continue to evaluate and enhance how the agency communicates measurable data to best inform how our officers and special agents perform their law enforcement missions in accordance with departmental and agency priorities.” — ICE Deputy Director and Senior Official Performing the Duties of the Director Patrick J. Lechleitner 

 --> 

 Arrest Statistics
 ERO enforces laws by arresting immigration violators in the interior of the United States. It relies on statutory law enforcement authority to identify and arrest aliens who may present threats to national security or public safety, or who otherwise undermine the integrity of U.S. immigration laws. ERO uses targeted, intelligence-driven operations to prioritize its enforcement actions in ways that help protect communities nationwide. While ERO primarily conducts administrative arrests of aliens it has probable cause to believe are removable from the United States, it also has the authority to execute criminal arrest warrants and initiate prosecutions for criminal activity, including immigration-related crimes. ERO officers assigned to task forces also help target and apprehend foreign fugitives in the United States who are wanted for crimes here and abroad by working with domestic and international partners.
 Arrests by country of citizenship and criminal history: ERO arrests are broken down by country of citizenship and categories of criminal history that include people with: U.S. criminal convictions.
 Pending criminal charges in the United States.
 No convictions or pending charges but who have broken U.S. immigration laws including visa overstays and Visa Waiver Program violators.*

*This category includes those who have repeatedly violated U.S. law by reentering after deportation, immigration fugitives with an executable final order of removal, and international fugitives wanted for crimes committed abroad.
 For fiscal years 2021 and 2022, this category also includes individuals apprehended while attempting to unlawfully enter the United States after January 1, 2021.

 ERO arrests over time: Historically, ERO most commonly arrests immigration violators with convictions involving DUI, drug possession, assault and criminal (non-civil) traffic offenses such as hit-and-run or leaving the scene of an accident.
 Arrests by Area of Responsibility (AOR): ERO has 24 field offices, which are geographic areas of responsibility , around the country, each headed by a field office director.

 Maintenance Alert

 Due to scheduled maintenance, the ICE Data Tables may be temporarily unavailable.

--> 

 Detention Statistics
 ERO oversees the civil immigration detention of one of the most diverse and rapidly changing detained populations in the world. The ERO Headquarters Custody Management and ICE Health Service Corps divisions help officers in the field manage the detained population and ensure detained aliens’ health and safety, ensure compliance with ICE’s detention standards, and provide medical care — including mental health care — to detained individuals.
 ICE detains individuals as necessary, including to secure their presence for immigration proceedings and removal from the United States. ICE also detains those who are subject to mandatory detention under U.S. immigration law and those a supervisor has determined are public safety or flight risks.
 After ICE arrests and processes individuals for administrative immigration violations or CBP and other state, local and federal law enforcement partners turn them over to ICE, officials may detain them while their immigration cases are pending or release them under a form of supervision. Both ICE and the Department of Justice’s Executive Office for Immigration Review — the office that oversees the immigration court system — can impact custody status at various points during a alien's immigration proceedings.
 Officials make custody determinations on an individual basis, taking into account all facets of a person’s situation, including their immigration history and criminal records. Authorities also consider family ties, humanitarian issues and whether a person may be a flight risk.
 Whenever possible, ICE seeks to house detained individuals within the geographical areas of their arrests to minimize their time in ICE custody and keep them close to family, friends and legal representatives.
 Most detained individuals are transfers from CBP following arrests at the border. ICE is legally obligated to detain some of these people, including those with certain criminal histories.
 If an alien or their representative believes they should not be subject to enforcement, detention or removal, they should contact their local ERO field office to request a case review or initiate the ICE Case Review process. People who want to contact ICE about their cases should first notify their local ERO field office via email with supporting documentation for an initial review.
 Detention by country of citizenship and criminal history: Detained individuals are categorized in the following ways: Individuals with criminal convictions.
 Individuals with pending criminal charges.
 Those with no convictions or pending charges but who have broken U.S. immigration laws.*

 Detention Management 

 Detention Management

 U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) manages the nation’s civil immigration detention system and oversees one of the most highly transient and diverse populations of any detention system in the world. 

 Detention Standards
 Regardless of whether detention facilities are owned and operated by ICE, a state or local entity, or a contractor, all facilities housing ICE detainees must comply with one of several sets of detention standards which describe a facility’s immigration detention responsibilities, explain what detainee services a facility must provide, and identify what a facility must do to ensure a safe and secure detention environment for staff and aliens in detention:
 2026 National Detention Standards 
 2025 National Detention Standards 
 Non-Dedicated Intergovernmental Detention Standards (NDIDS) 
 PBNDS 2011 
 NDS 2019 
 Family Residential Standards 2020 
 Temporary Housing Standards 
 Detention Facility Oversight
 To ensure compliance with each contract’s terms and conditions and the applicable detention standards, ICE and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employ a robust, multilevel oversight and compliance program. ERO monitors detention conditions through daily on-site compliance reviews to identify deficiencies, areas of concern, contract and facility issues, and to facilitate corrective actions. All facilities that house aliens detained by ICE are required to follow a strict set of detention standards.
 Detention Policies
 Detention is non-punitive. Once an alien is transferred to ICE custody, the agency makes a custody determination. ICE uses its limited detention resources to detain aliens to secure their presence for immigration proceedings or removal from the United States — as well as those that are subject to mandatory detention, as outlined by the Immigration and Nationality Act, or those that ICE determines are a public safety or flight risk during the custody determination process.
 When an alien is not subject to mandatory detention or is not deemed to be a public safety or flight risk, ICE exercises its discretion in making custody determinations to release aliens with conditions. These custody decisions are made on a case-by-case basis and after considering the totality of circumstances — primarily considering risk of flight, national security threat and risk to public safety.
 ICE also takes other factors into consideration — including when an alien has a serious medical condition, is the primary caregiver of minor children, or other humanitarian considerations.
 Family Detention
 In the past, ICE housed family units — which contain adult alien parents or legal guardians accompanied by their own juvenile alien children — in its Family Residential Centers (FRCs). In March 2021, ICE converted the Family Residential Centers (FRCs) from an over-72-hour residential program to an under-72-hour residential/staging program called Family Staging Centers (FSCs).
 In FY 2022, ICE opted to shift its resources again to increase efficiencies in Alternatives to Detention (ATD) enrollment for family units. ICE worked to co-locate with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to assist with limiting any processing slowdowns.
 Once the agency determined that the FSCs were at a lower-than-expected capacity, ICE took steps to increase the use of the bed space for single adults and eventually, ICE stopped housing families entirely by December 2021.
 Custody and Care of Unaccompanied Children (UC)
 ICE does not detain unaccompanied children — except in rare instances.
 As part of the restructuring of the former Immigration and Naturalization Service, the Homeland Security Act of 2002 transferred the responsibilities related to the care and custody of unaccompanied undocumented children to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR).
 In accordance with the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act (TVPRA) of 2008, ERO coordinates closely with inter-departmental partners to ensure the timely and safe transfer of unaccompanied alien children from DHS to HHS ORR custody.
 Detention Statistics
 ICE provides the following custody data below. The data tables are searchable and sortable, and worksheets are protected to ensure their accuracy and reliability. ICE confirms the integrity of the data as published on this site but cannot attest to subsequent transmissions. Data may fluctuate until it is locked at the conclusion of the fiscal year.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Non-Detained Docket (NDD) - EveryCRSReport.com 

 Internet Explorer version 8 or any modern web browser is required to use this website, sorry. 

 Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Non-Detained Docket (NDD)

 April 24, 2026
 IF13208 

 Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Non-Detained Docket (NDD) 

 April 24, 2026
 (IF13208)

 Background

 The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA, Title 8 of the U .S. Code ) authorizes and sometimes requires the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to detain aliens ( foreign nationals ) who are subject to removal from the United States. This authority allows DHS to detain aliens who pose a threat to public safety, ensures that such individuals appear at immigration removal hearings, and permits DHS to remove an individual more effectively after an order of removal has been issued. Detained aliens represent what is known as the detained docket . However, DHS has broad discretion to release from custody those aliens who are not subject to mandatory detention or do not pose a threat or flight risk. These individuals represent the non-detained docket (NDD) .

 Supervision of aliens on the detained and the non-detained docke ts is the responsibility of Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) within DHS's Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) . ERO may arrest any alien who is believed to have violated U.S. immigration laws and remove any alien who has received a final removal order . The INA generally requires detention for applicants for admission who are removable, aliens removable on specified criminal and terrorist-related grounds, and those with final removal orders.

 The INA also grants DHS discretion to either detain or release from custody all other aliens in pending removal proceedings. After ICE arrests an alien not subject to mandatory detention, an immigration officer makes an initial custody determination and may make further determinations during the course of formal removal proceedings, based on standards and criteria promulgated by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ). 

 A lien s may be detained in an ICE facility or released on bond or conditional parole ; these individuals become part of the NDD . In any case, a lien s must attend all subsequent proceedings before an immigration judge (IJ) within DOJ ' s Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) . Detained aliens may request a review of the custody determination during a bond hearing before an IJ, unless they are subject to detention without bond by federal law.

 ICE's detention capacity limits the number of detainees that can be held at any given time. ICE currently oversees detainees in over 200 ICE-owned, private, state, and local facilities that house from fewer than 5 aliens to more than 2,000. ICE data indicate that 6 6,978 individuals were detained as of April 9, 2026. Between FY1996 and FY2025, the average annual total of detained individuals ranged from about 9,000 to 60,000. Currently, ICE possesses detention bedspace capacity for roughly 70,000 individuals and has considered plans to expand this capacity to over 90,000 in FY2026. 

 In contrast, the NDD refers to aliens who are subject to removal but are not detained . The docket includes individuals at any stage in the removal process . Individuals on the NDD remain under ICE supervision to help ensure that they regularly check in, comply with release conditions, attend court hearings, and comply with removal if so ordered. 

 The NDD Population

 Generally, the NDD population consists of aliens that 
 have been released at ICE's discretion following an initial or subsequent custody determination (as discussed previously); 

 are currently incarcerated in federal, state, and local facilities while serving sentences for criminal offenses; 

 have final removal orders but were granted temporary protection through withholding of removal or the Convention Against Torture (CAT) ;

 have final removal orders and are in the process of being repatriated; 

 have final removal orders but cannot be repatriated because their origin countries do not cooperate with the United States; 

 have final removal orders but absconded into the United States as fugitives ; and 

 unbeknownst to ICE, have voluntarily departed the United States or died and remain on the NDD erroneously. 
 ICE's most recently reported NDD population size of 7.3 million reflects its count of non-detained aliens as of February 26, 2026 ( Figure 1 ). All such individuals have been processed by ICE, including an estimated 1.6 million with final orders of removal . The NDD count relies on a cumulative list of removable aliens that is continuously updated; thus, it excludes those with a confirmed departure or death. Some aliens have been on the NDD for decades; others have been placed on it more recently. A fraction of NDD individuals are enrolled in ICE's Alternatives to Detention (ATD) program, which involves more intensive supervision than other NDD individuals who, in addition to attending all court hearings, typically must check in once a year with ICE. Currently, 180,000 individuals are on ATD.

 NDD Trends

 The NDD has more than tripled since FY2016 ( Figure 1 ). Recent NDD growth reflects high numbers of encounters (apprehensions) of aliens by the U.S. Border Patrol (USBP), part of DHS's Customs and Border Protection (CBP). From FY2016 through FY2020, annual USBP encounters at the Southwest border averaged about 470,000, and the NDD grew during that period from 2.2 million to 3.3 million unauthorized aliens. From FY2021 through FY2024, average annual encounters more than quadrupled to 1.9 million, boosting the NDD from 3.7 million to 7.7 million individuals. Since FY2025 (as of March 2026 ), USBP encounters have declined substantially. Increased ICE enforcement actions and removals that have prompted unauthorized aliens to self-deport have also reduced the NDD. Reportedly , about 72,000 aliens as of March 2026 have used a CBP incentive-based program to facilitate their voluntary departure and many others have left of their own accord.

 Figure 1. Estimated NDD Population, FY2016-FY2026*

 Source: FY2016: DHS OIG-17-51; FY2017-FY2019: ICE ERO Annual Report, FY2019; FY2020-FY2023: ICE Annual Report, FY2023; FY2024: ICE Annual Report, FY2024; FY2025-FY2026: ICE Office of Legislative Affairs.

 Notes: FY2026 * figure as of February 26, 2026.

 How the NDD Fluctuates

 The NDD increases with alien apprehensions and arrests and decreases when aliens are removed from the United States, or granted immigration relief (e.g., asylum) following immigration court proceedings. When border encounters are high, immigration officers may use their discretion to supervise individuals on the NDD instead of in limited detention space. In addition, ICE cannot remove aliens with final removal orders if their countries of citizenship restrict returns of their nationals ; this

## Executive Summary

- ICE's own accounting to Congress shows 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions on the agency's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, none of them in ICE custody, including 13,099 convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault and 13,423 convicted of weapons offenses.

**FSI Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14** | By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy | Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive Summary

- ICE's own accounting to Congress shows 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions on the agency's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, none of them in ICE custody, including 13,099 convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault and 13,423 convicted of weapons offenses.

{"content": "# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14** | Founders' Square Institute
**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy** | Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- ICE reported to Congress that 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions were on its non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, none of them in ICE custody. They included 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault and 13,423 convicted of weapons offenses.
- Noncitizens accounted for 44 percent of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2025 (28,886 of 66,662), and 92 percent of those noncitizens were illegal aliens. In fiscal 2024 the noncitizen share was 34.7 percent.
- Sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 ICE detainers in 2025, and ICE records show 25,283 detainers declined from October 2022 through February 2025. Congress should fund criminal-alien detention, condition federal grants on detainer compliance, codify the 287(g) program and mandate public reporting on releases.

## 1. The non-detained docket

The clearest measure of what weak interior enforcement costs the public is the list ICE keeps of removable aliens it is not holding. In a September 2024 letter to Congress, ICE reported that as of July 21, 2024, its national docket carried 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories: 435,719 convicted criminals, plus another 226,847 with pending criminal charges. Of the convicted criminals, 425,431 were on the non-detained docket, which means not one of them was in ICE custody.

The convictions on that list are not minor. Grouped by ICE's most serious charge categories, the non-detained docket that day carried 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault, 62,231 convicted of assault, 13,423 convicted of weapons offenses and 56,533 convicted of dangerous-drug offenses. Every homicide conviction stands for a victim. On this list alone there are 13,099.

The docket also dwarfs the system built to contain it. The Congressional Research Service reports that the non-detained docket stood at 7.3 million aliens as of February 2026, more than triple its size in 2016, while ICE holds bedspace for roughly 70,000 detainees and had 66,978 people in custody on April 9, 2026. Detention capacity is the constant; the docket is the variable. Aliens on the non-detained docket are, in the typical case, subject to no supervision beyond an annual check-in with ICE.

The docket has victims. Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was murdered while jogging on the University of Georgia campus in Athens on Feb. 22, 2024. Her killer, Jose Ibarra, was a Venezuelan national who crossed the border illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and was released pending his immigration case. He was convicted on all 10 counts in November 2024 and sentenced to life without parole. Nothing about his path through the system was unusual. That is the point.

## 2. Federal sentencing

The federal courts tell the same story at the other end of the process. Of the 66,662 individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2025, 28,886, or 44 percent, were not U.S. citizens. Nine in 10 of those noncitizens, 92 percent, were illegal aliens. A year earlier, noncitizens were 34.7 percent of everyone sentenced, 21,304 people, of whom 88.7 percent were illegal aliens.

The most common guideline under which noncitizens are sentenced is immigration: unlawful entry and unlawful reentry, offenses that by definition require illegal presence in the country. Drug trafficking is the second most common, at 17.6 percent of noncitizen sentences in fiscal 2024 and 12 percent in fiscal 2025.

These are federal numbers, and federal numbers are a floor. Most crime is prosecuted in state court, where the immigration status of defendants is generally not recorded at all. What the federal data establish is scale: in a single fiscal year, tens of thousands of illegal aliens were sentenced in federal court, and noncitizens were 44 percent of the entire federal sentencing docket.

## 3. What the Texas data show

Texas keeps the best state-level record of criminal-alien offending, because its Department of Public Safety records the immigration status of people booked into its jails and follows up as more of them are identified in prison. No other state keeps comparable records.

Read in full, the Texas data do not flatter illegal immigration. The Center for Immigration Studies, analyzing DPS conviction records, concludes that illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates than the general population for the most serious crimes, homicide and sexual assault included, once offenders identified as illegal immigrants only after incarceration are counted. The reason is straightforward: DPS does not learn every offender's immigration status at booking, and analyses that use only booking-stage identifications classify as native-born a significant number of offenders whom Texas later identifies as illegal immigrants. The undercount falls hardest on the most serious crimes, where sentences are longest and identification most often comes late.

That is a methodological dispute, but it is a dispute about how many victims illegal immigration produces, in the one state that keeps the records capable of answering it.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers

A detainer is ICE's request that a jail hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours after he would otherwise be released, so that ICE can take him into custody. Sanctuary policies instruct jails not to honor them, and the Department of Homeland Security is now counting the consequences. Testifying before the House Judiciary Committee on March 4, 2026, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem reported that sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 detainers in 2025. ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies show 25,283 detainers declined from fiscal 2023 through Feb. 6, 2025, a count that grew every year, and more than 1,400 instances in which a jail failed to give ICE adequate notice before releasing an alien. California's jails alone declined 13,025 detainers, 52 percent of the total.

Jose Ibarra passed through this door as well. New York police arrested him in August 2023 on a charge of endangering a child and released him before ICE could lodge a detainer, in a city that does not honor them. Six months later, Laken Riley was dead.

A declined detainer is a decision, made by a public official, to release a removable criminal alien rather than transfer him to federal custody. The federal data show that officials made that decision more than 17,000 times last year.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund criminal-alien detention.** Appropriate what ICE needs to carry out its planned expansion beyond 90,000 beds in fiscal 2026, and direct that the added capacity be reserved first for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, including by taking custody as they complete criminal sentences.
2. **Condition federal grants on detainer compliance.** Make honoring ICE detainers and giving timely notice of release conditions of eligibility for Justice Department and DHS law-enforcement grants, and direct the attorney general to withhold funds from jurisdictions that decline.
3. **Codify and fund 287(g).** Write the 287(g) program into statute, beyond the reach of any future administration, and appropriate training funds for every willing law-enforcement agency. ICE now has 2,679 agreements in force; there is no reason the number cannot double.
4. **Require public reporting.** Direct DHS to publish quarterly, and by jurisdiction, the number of declined detainers, failed notifications and criminal aliens released from state and local custody, and to keep reporting the criminal composition of the non-detained docket.

Congress does not need new evidence. The federal government has been producing it for years, in letters, sentencing data and testimony. It needs to act on it.

*All figures are dated and sourced in the data appendix accompanying this brief.*

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14** | Founders' Square Institute
**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy** | Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- ICE reported to Congress that 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions were on its non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, none of them in ICE custody. They included 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault and 13,423 convicted of weapons offenses.
- Noncitizens accounted for 44 percent of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2025 (28,886 of 66,662), and 92 percent of those noncitizens were illegal aliens. In fiscal 2024 the noncitizen share was 34.7 percent.
- Sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 ICE detainers in 2025, and ICE records show 25,283 detainers declined from October 2022 through February 2025. Congress should fund criminal-alien detention, condition federal grants on detainer compliance, codify the 287(g) program and mandate public reporting on releases.

## 1. The non-detained docket

The clearest measure of what weak interior enforcement costs the public is the list ICE keeps of removable aliens it is not holding. In a September 2024 letter to Congress, ICE reported that as of July 21, 2024, its national docket carried 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories: 435,719 convicted criminals, plus another 226,847 with pending criminal charges. Of the convicted criminals, 425,431 were on the non-detained docket, which means not one of them was in ICE custody.

The convictions on that list are not minor. Grouped by ICE's most serious charge categories, the non-detained docket that day carried 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault, 62,231 convicted of assault, 13,423 convicted of weapons offenses and 56,533 convicted of dangerous-drug offenses. Every homicide conviction stands for a victim. On this list alone there are 13,099.

The docket also dwarfs the system built to contain it. The Congressional Research Service reports that the non-detained docket stood at 7.3 million aliens as of February 2026, more than triple its size in 2016, while ICE holds bedspace for roughly 70,000 detainees and had 66,978 people in custody on April 9, 2026. Detention capacity is the constant; the docket is the variable. Aliens on the non-detained docket are, in the typical case, subject to no supervision beyond an annual check-in with ICE.

The docket has victims. Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was murdered while jogging on the University of Georgia campus in Athens on Feb. 22, 2024. Her killer, Jose Ibarra, was a Venezuelan national who crossed the border illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and was released pending his immigration case. He was convicted on all 10 counts in November 2024 and sentenced to life without parole. Nothing about his path through the system was unusual. That is the point.

## 2. Federal sentencing

The federal courts tell the same story at the other end of the process. Of the 66,662 individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2025, 28,886, or 44 percent, were not U.S. citizens. Nine in 10 of those noncitizens, 92 percent, were illegal aliens. A year earlier, noncitizens were 34.7 percent of everyone sentenced, 21,304 people, of whom 88.7 percent were illegal aliens.

The most common guideline under which noncitizens are sentenced is immigration, unlawful entry and unlawful reentry, offenses that by definition require illegal presence in the country. Drug trafficking is the second most common, at 17.6 percent of noncitizen sentences in fiscal 2024 and 12 percent in fiscal 2025.

These are federal numbers, and federal numbers are a floor. Most crime is prosecuted in state court, where the immigration status of defendants is generally not recorded at all. What the federal data establish is scale: in a single fiscal year, tens of thousands of illegal aliens were sentenced in federal court, and noncitizens were 44 percent of the entire federal sentencing docket.

## 3. What the Texas data show

Texas keeps the best state-level record of criminal-alien offending, because its Department of Public Safety records the immigration status of people booked into its jails and follows up as more are identified in prison. No other state keeps comparable records.

Read in full, the Texas data do not flatter illegal immigration. The Center for Immigration Studies, analyzing DPS conviction records, concludes that illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates than the general population for the most serious crimes, homicide and sexual assault included, once offenders identified as illegal immigrants only after incarceration are counted. The reason is straightforward: DPS does not learn every offender's immigration status at booking, and studies that use only booking-stage identifications end up classifying as native-born a significant number of offenders whom Texas later identifies as illegal immigrants. The undercount falls hardest on the most serious crimes, where sentences are longest and identification most often comes late.

That is a methodological dispute, but it is a dispute about how many victims illegal immigration produces, in the one state that keeps the records to answer it.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers

A detainer is ICE's request that a jail hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours after he would otherwise be released, so that ICE can take him into custody. Sanctuary policies instruct jails not to honor them. DHS is now counting the consequences. Testifying before the House Judiciary Committee on March 4, 2026, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem reported that sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 detainers in 2025. ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies show 25,283 detainers declined from fiscal 2023 through Feb. 6, 2025, a count that grew every year, plus more than 1,400 instances in which a jail released a deportable alien without notifying ICE at all. California's jails alone declined 13,025 detainers, 52 percent of the total.

Jose Ibarra passed through this door as well. New York police arrested him in August 2023 on a charge of endangering a child and released him before ICE could lodge a detainer, in a city that does not honor them. Six months later, Laken Riley was dead.

A declined detainer is a decision, made by a public official, to release a removable criminal alien rather than transfer him to federal custody. The federal data show officials made that decision more than 17,000 times last year.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund criminal-alien detention.** Appropriate what ICE needs to carry out its planned expansion beyond 90,000 beds in fiscal 2026, and direct that the added capacity be reserved first for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, including by taking custody as they complete criminal sentences.
2. **Condition federal grants on detainer compliance.** Make honoring ICE detainers and giving timely notice of release conditions of eligibility for Justice Department and DHS law enforcement grants, and direct the attorney general to withhold funds from jurisdictions that decline.
3. **Codify and fund 287(g).** Write the 287(g) program into statute, beyond the reach of any future administration, and appropriate training funds for every willing law enforcement agency. ICE now has 2,679 agreements; there is no reason the number cannot double.
4. **Require public reporting.** Direct DHS to publish quarterly, and by jurisdiction, the number of declined detainers, failed notifications and criminal aliens released from state and local custody, and to keep reporting the criminal composition of the non-detained docket.

Congress does not need new evidence. The federal government has been producing it for years, in letters, sentencing data and testimony. It needs to act on it.

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14** | Founders' Square Institute
**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy** | Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- ICE reported to Congress that 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions were on its non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, none of them in ICE custody. They included 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault and 13,423 convicted of weapons offenses.
- Noncitizens accounted for 44 percent of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2025 (28,886 of 66,662), and 92 percent of those noncitizens were illegal aliens. In fiscal 2024 the noncitizen share was 34.7 percent.
- Sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 ICE detainers in 2025, and ICE records show 25,283 detainers declined from October 2022 through February 2025. Congress should fund criminal-alien detention, condition federal grants on detainer compliance, codify the 287(g) program and mandate public reporting on releases.

## 1. The non-detained docket

The clearest measure of what weak interior enforcement costs the public is the list ICE keeps of removable aliens it is not holding. In a September 2024 letter to Congress, ICE reported that as of July 21, 2024, its national docket carried 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories: 435,719 convicted criminals, plus another 226,847 with pending criminal charges. Of the convicted criminals, 425,431 were on the non-detained docket, which means not one of them was in ICE custody.

The convictions on that list are not minor. Grouped by ICE's most serious charge categories, the non-detained docket that day carried 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault, 62,231 convicted of assault, 13,423 convicted of weapons offenses and 56,533 convicted of dangerous-drug offenses. Every homicide conviction stands for a victim. On this list alone there are 13,099.

The docket also dwarfs the system built to contain it. The Congressional Research Service reports that the non-detained docket stood at 7.3 million aliens as of February 2026, more than triple its size in 2016, while ICE holds bedspace for roughly 70,000 detainees and had 66,978 people in custody on April 9, 2026. Detention capacity is the constant; the docket is the variable. Aliens on the non-detained docket are, in the typical case, subject to no supervision beyond an annual check-in with ICE.

The docket has victims. Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was murdered while jogging on the University of Georgia campus in Athens on Feb. 22, 2024. Her killer, Jose Ibarra, was a Venezuelan national who crossed the border illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and was released pending his immigration case. He was convicted on all 10 counts in November 2024 and sentenced to life without parole. Nothing about his path through the system was unusual. That is the point.

## 2. Federal sentencing

The federal courts tell the same story at the other end of the process. Of the 66,662 individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2025, 28,886, or 44 percent, were not U.S. citizens. Nine in 10 of those noncitizens, 92 percent, were illegal aliens. A year earlier, noncitizens were 34.7 percent of everyone sentenced, 21,304 people, of whom 88.7 percent were illegal aliens.

The most common guideline under which noncitizens are sentenced is immigration, unlawful entry and unlawful reentry, offenses that by definition require illegal presence in the country. Drug trafficking is the second most common, at 17.6 percent of noncitizen sentences in fiscal 2024 and 12 percent in fiscal 2025.

These are federal numbers, and federal numbers are a floor. Most crime is prosecuted in state court, where the immigration status of defendants is generally not recorded at all. What the federal data establish is scale: in a single fiscal year, tens of thousands of illegal aliens were sentenced in federal court, and noncitizens were 44 percent of the entire federal sentencing docket.

## 3. What the Texas data show

Texas keeps the best state-level record of criminal-alien offending, because its Department of Public Safety records the immigration status of people booked into its jails and follows up as more are identified in prison. No other state keeps comparable records.

Read in full, the Texas data do not flatter illegal immigration. The Center for Immigration Studies, analyzing DPS conviction records, concludes that illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates than the general population for the most serious crimes, homicide and sexual assault included, once offenders identified as illegal immigrants only after incarceration are counted. The reason is straightforward: DPS does not learn every offender's immigration status at booking, and studies that use only booking-stage identifications end up classifying as native-born a significant number of offenders whom Texas later identifies as illegal immigrants. The undercount falls hardest on the most serious crimes, where sentences are longest and identification most often comes late.

That is a methodological dispute, but it is a dispute about how many victims illegal immigration produces, in the one state that keeps the records to answer it.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers

A detainer is ICE's request that a jail hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours after he would otherwise be released, so that ICE can take him into custody. Sanctuary policies instruct jails not to honor them. DHS is now counting the consequences. Testifying before the House Judiciary Committee on March 4, 2026, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem reported that sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 detainers in 2025. ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies show 25,283 detainers declined from fiscal 2023 through Feb. 6, 2025, a count that grew every year, plus more than 1,400 instances in which a jail released a deportable alien without notifying ICE at all. California's jails alone declined 13,025 detainers, 52 percent of the total.

Jose Ibarra passed through this door as well. New York police arrested him in August 2023 on a charge of endangering a child and released him before ICE could lodge a detainer, in a city that does not honor them. Six months later, Laken Riley was dead.

A declined detainer is a decision, made by a public official, to release a removable criminal alien rather than transfer him to federal custody. The federal data show officials made that decision more than 17,000 times last year.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund criminal-alien detention.** Appropriate what ICE needs to carry out its planned expansion beyond 90,000 beds in fiscal 2026, and direct that the added capacity be reserved first for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, including by taking custody as they complete criminal sentences.
2. **Condition federal grants on detainer compliance.** Make honoring ICE detainers and giving timely notice of release conditions of eligibility for Justice Department and DHS law enforcement grants, and direct the attorney general to withhold funds from jurisdictions that decline.
3. **Codify and fund 287(g).** Write the 287(g) program into statute, beyond the reach of any future administration, and appropriate training funds for every willing law enforcement agency. ICE now has 2,679 agreements; there is no reason the number cannot double.
4. **Require public reporting.** Direct DHS to publish quarterly, and by jurisdiction, the number of declined detainers, failed notifications and criminal aliens released from state and local custody, and to keep reporting the criminal composition of the non-detained docket.

Congress does not need new evidence. The federal government has been producing it for years, in letters, sentencing data and testimony. It needs to act on it.

*All figures are dated and sourced in the data appendix accompanying this brief.*

**Media contact: Office of Communications, Founders' Square Institute [contact details to be inserted]**

# Federal Data Show 13,099 Convicted Killers Outside ICE Custody: FSI Brief

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026 — The Founders' Square Institute today released Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Brett Kessler, senior fellow for immigration policy. The brief draws on the federal government's own records to document the public-safety cost of weak interior enforcement.

The core findings:

- ICE reported to Congress that as of July 21, 2024, 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions were on the agency's non-detained docket, none in ICE custody, including 13,099 convicted of homicide and 15,811 of sexual assault.
- Noncitizens accounted for 44 percent of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2025, and 92 percent of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 ICE detainers in 2025, according to Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem's March testimony to Congress.

"Every number in this brief comes from the government's own records," Kessler said. "More than 425,000 convicted criminals sit on ICE's non-detained docket, nearly 13,100 of them killers, and sanctuary cities refused almost 18,000 detainers last year alone. These are policy choices, and Congress can reverse them."

The brief urges Congress to fund ICE's planned detention expansion beyond 90,000 beds and reserve that capacity for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket; to condition federal law-enforcement grants on honoring ICE detainers; to write the 287(g) program, now 2,679 agreements strong, into statute; and to require quarterly public reporting, by jurisdiction, of declined detainers and criminal-alien releases.

"Congress does not need new evidence. The federal government has been producing it for years," Kessler said. "It needs to act on it."

Brief No. 14, its data appendix and a one-page fact sheet for Hill offices are available from the FSI Office of Communications.

The Founders' Square Institute is a public-policy think tank in Washington, D.C.

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14** | Founders' Square Institute
**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy** | Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- ICE reported to Congress that 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions were on its non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, none of them in ICE custody. They included 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault and 13,423 convicted of weapons offenses.
- The U.S. Sentencing Commission reports that noncitizens accounted for 44 percent of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2025 (28,886 of 66,662), 92 percent of them illegal aliens; in fiscal 2024 the share was 34.7 percent.
- Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem testified that sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 ICE detainers in 2025, and ICE records show 25,283 detainers declined from October 2022 through February 2025. Congress should fund criminal-alien detention, condition federal grants on detainer compliance, codify the 287(g) program and mandate public reporting on releases.

## 1. The non-detained docket

The clearest measure of what weak interior enforcement costs the public is the list ICE keeps of removable aliens it is not holding. In a September 2024 letter to Congress, ICE reported that as of July 21, 2024, its national docket carried 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories: 435,719 convicted criminals, plus another 226,847 with pending criminal charges. Of the convicted criminals, 425,431 were on the non-detained docket, which means not one of them was in ICE custody.

The convictions on that list are not minor. Grouped by ICE's most serious charge categories, the non-detained docket that day carried 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault, 62,231 convicted of assault, 13,423 convicted of weapons offenses and 56,533 convicted of dangerous-drug offenses. Every homicide conviction stands for a victim. On this list alone there are 13,099.

The docket also dwarfs the system built to contain it. The Congressional Research Service reports that the non-detained docket stood at 7.3 million aliens as of February 2026, more than triple its size in 2016, while ICE holds bedspace for roughly 70,000 detainees and had 66,978 people in custody on April 9, 2026. Detention capacity is the constant; the docket is the variable. Aliens on the non-detained docket are, in the typical case, subject to no supervision beyond an annual check-in with ICE.

The docket has victims. Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was murdered while jogging on the University of Georgia campus in Athens on Feb. 22, 2024. Her killer, Jose Ibarra, was a Venezuelan national who crossed the border illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and was released pending his immigration case. He was convicted on all 10 counts in November 2024 and sentenced to life without parole. Nothing about his path through the system was unusual. That is the point.

## 2. Federal sentencing

The federal courts tell the same story at the other end of the process. The U.S. Sentencing Commission reports that of the 66,662 individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2025, 28,886, or 44 percent, were not U.S. citizens. Nine in 10 of those noncitizens, 92 percent, were illegal aliens. A year earlier, noncitizens were 34.7 percent of everyone sentenced, 21,304 people, of whom 88.7 percent were illegal aliens.

The most common guideline under which noncitizens are sentenced is immigration: unlawful entry and unlawful reentry, offenses that by definition require illegal presence in the country. Drug trafficking is the second most common, at 17.6 percent of noncitizen sentences in fiscal 2024 and 12 percent in fiscal 2025.

These are federal numbers, and federal numbers are a floor. Most crime is prosecuted in state court, where the immigration status of defendants is generally not recorded at all. What the federal data establish is scale: in a single fiscal year, tens of thousands of illegal aliens were sentenced in federal court, and noncitizens were 44 percent of the entire federal sentencing docket.

## 3. What the Texas data show

Texas keeps the best state-level record of criminal-alien offending, because its Department of Public Safety records the immigration status of people booked into its jails and follows up as more of them are identified in prison. No other state keeps comparable records.

Read in full, the Texas data do not flatter illegal immigration. The Center for Immigration Studies, analyzing DPS conviction records, concludes that illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates than the general population for the most serious crimes, homicide and sexual assault included, once offenders identified as illegal immigrants only after incarceration are counted. The reason is straightforward: DPS does not learn every offender's immigration status at booking, and analyses that use only booking-stage identifications classify as native-born a significant number of offenders whom Texas later identifies as illegal immigrants. The undercount falls hardest on the most serious crimes, where sentences are longest and identification most often comes late.

That is a methodological dispute, but it is a dispute about how many victims illegal immigration produces, in the one state that keeps the records capable of answering it.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers

A detainer is ICE's request that a jail hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours after he would otherwise be released, so that ICE can take him into custody. Sanctuary policies instruct jails not to honor them, and the Department of Homeland Security is now counting the consequences. Testifying before the House Judiciary Committee on March 4, 2026, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem reported that sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 detainers in 2025. ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies show 25,283 detainers declined from fiscal 2023 through Feb. 6, 2025, a count that grew every year, and more than 1,400 instances in which a jail failed to give ICE adequate notice before releasing an alien. California's jails alone declined 13,025 detainers, 52 percent of the total.

Jose Ibarra passed through this door as well. New York police arrested him in August 2023 on a charge of endangering a child and released him before ICE could lodge a detainer, in a city that does not honor them. Six months later, Laken Riley was dead.

A declined detainer is a decision, made by a public official, to release a removable criminal alien rather than transfer him to federal custody. The federal data show that officials made that decision more than 17,000 times last year.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund criminal-alien detention.** Appropriate what ICE needs to carry out its planned expansion beyond 90,000 beds in fiscal 2026, and direct that the added capacity be reserved first for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, including by taking custody as they complete criminal sentences.
2. **Condition federal grants on detainer compliance.** Make honoring ICE detainers and giving timely notice of release conditions of eligibility for Justice Department and DHS law-enforcement grants, and direct the attorney general to withhold funds from jurisdictions that decline.
3. **Codify and fund 287(g).** Write the 287(g) program into statute, beyond the reach of any future administration, and appropriate training funds for every willing law-enforcement agency. ICE now has 2,679 agreements in force; there is no reason the number cannot double.
4. **Require public reporting.** Direct DHS to publish quarterly, and by jurisdiction, the number of declined detainers, failed notifications and criminal aliens released from state and local custody, and to keep reporting the criminal composition of the non-detained docket.

Congress does not need new evidence. The federal government has been producing it for years, in letters, sentencing data and testimony. It needs to act on it.

*All figures are dated and sourced in the data appendix accompanying this brief.*

# Data Appendix: Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

**"Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show"** | By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy | Founders' Square Institute | Oct. 27, 2026

Source lines follow FSI Publications Style Sheet rev. 3, section C1 (Agency/author, Title, Date, URL). Population, timeframe and methodology notes (style sheet B1) appear beneath each table. One table per figure used in the brief; context tables are labeled as such.

---

## Table A1. ICE dockets: noncitizens with criminal histories, as of July 21, 2024

| Measure | Noncitizens |
|---|---:|
| National docket (detained and non-detained), total with criminal histories | 662,566 |
| Convicted criminals on the national docket | 435,719 |
| With pending criminal charges | 226,847 |
| **Convicted criminals on the non-detained docket (not in ICE custody)** | **425,431** |

Non-detained docket, by most serious conviction category:

| Most serious category | Individuals |
|---|---:|
| Homicide | 13,099 |
| Sexual assault | 15,811 |
| Assault | 62,231 |
| Weapons offenses | 13,423 |
| Dangerous drugs | 56,533 |
| Traffic-related offenses | 77,074 |
| Stolen vehicles | 2,663 |

Source: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Acting Director Patrick J. Lechleitner, letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, Sep. 25, 2024, https://homeland.house.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/24-01143-ICEs-Signed-Response-to-Representative-Tony-Gonzales.pdf

Notes:
- "Non-detained" means not held in ICE detention; it does not mean at large. Per DHS/ICE statements in September and October 2024, the data span roughly four decades of records, covering individuals who entered under administrations of both parties, and the non-detained docket includes noncitizens serving sentences in federal, state and local custody. ICE did not report how many of the individuals counted in each category are currently incarcerated by another authority.
- Category figures count individuals whose most serious conviction falls in that category; individuals may have additional convictions.
- The letter responds to a March 13, 2024 request and reports docket data "as of July 21, 2024."

---

## Table A2. Federal sentencing: non-U.S. citizens, FY2024 and FY2025

| Measure | FY2024 | FY2025 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Individuals sentenced, all | 61,678 | 66,662 |
| Non-U.S. citizens sentenced | 21,304 | 28,886 |
| Noncitizen share of all individuals sentenced | 34.7% | 44% |
| Illegal aliens, share of noncitizens sentenced | 88.7% | 92% |
| Legal aliens, share of noncitizens sentenced | 8.5% | 6% |

| Average sentence, U.S. citizens | — | 71 months |

Sources: U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts on Federally Sentenced Non-U.S. Citizens, FY2024 (published 2025), https://www.ussc.gov/sites/default/files/pdf/research-and-publications/quick-facts/Non-Citizen_FY24.pdf; U.S. Sentencing Commission, Federally Sentenced Non-U.S. Citizens (Quick Facts), FY2025, accessed Oct. 16, 2026, https://www.ussc.gov/research/quick-facts/federally-sentenced-non-us-citizens

Notes:
- Fiscal years end Sept. 30. Federal sentences only; state prosecutions are excluded, and most crime is prosecuted in state court.
- Immigration offenses (unlawful entry, unlawful reentry) can be committed only by noncitizens, so the noncitizen share of the federal docket is driven largely by immigration prosecutions: 72.3 percent of noncitizen sentences in FY2024 and 79 percent in FY2025 were under the immigration guideline. Drug trafficking was second in both years.
- The noncitizen share of federal sentences fluctuates with prosecution priorities; it was 42.7 percent as far back as FY2018 (see Table A3). The brief reports FY2025 as the most recent full fiscal year and FY2024 as the prior-year comparison.
- USSC excludes cases with incomplete sentencing information; figures are as published by the Commission.

---

## Table A3. Context: noncitizens in federal sentencing and prison, FY2018-FY2023 (not cited in the brief)

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|

Sources: U.S. Government Accountability Office, Noncitizens in the U.S.: Public Information on Federal Incarcerations (GAO-24-107598), Oct. 3, 2024, https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-107598; U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts on Non-U.S. Citizen Offenders, FY2018, https://www.ussc.gov/sites/default/files/pdf/research-and-publications/quick-facts/Non-Citizens_FY18.pdf

Notes:
- GAO reports the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes declined 27 percent from FY2018 to FY2023, before the increases shown in Table A2 for FY2024 and FY2025.
- GAO counts include noncitizens sentenced in federal court for a felony or class A misdemeanor.

Notes:

## Table A6. 287(g) agreements with state and local law enforcement

| Measure | Value |
|---|---:|
| Active memorandums of agreement | 2,679 |
| Coverage | 38 states and 2 U.S. territories |
| Jail Enforcement Model agreements | 183 agencies, 29 states and 1 territory |
| Warrant Service Officer agreements | 572 agencies, 34 states |
| Task Force Model agreements | 1,924 agencies, 32 states and 2 territories |
| Active agreements, February 2026 | 1,412 |
| Agreements in 2019 | 45 |

Sources: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Delegation of Immigration Authority Section 287(g) Immigration and Nationality Act, updated Oct. 14, 2026, https://www.ice.gov/identify-and-arrest/287g; NPR, "Little-Used ICE Agreements With Local Police Have Exploded Under Trump," Feb. 17, 2026, https://www.npr.org/2026/02/17/nx-s1-5707449/local-police-immigration-cooperation-287g

Notes:
- Counts current as of Oct. 15, 2026, per ICE; agreements are added and terminated continuously.
- Model definitions per ICE: the Jail Enforcement Model lets designated officers identify and process removable aliens with pending or active criminal charges; the Warrant Service Officer model lets officers serve administrative warrants on aliens in custody; the Task Force Model lets officers exercise limited immigration authority during routine police duties or in ICE-led task forces.
- Growth since 2025 reflects Executive Order 14159 (Jan. 20, 2025), which directs ICE to authorize 287(g) agreements to the maximum extent permitted by law.

---

## Table A7. ICE detention and the non-detained docket

| Measure | Value | Date |
|---|---:|---|
| Non-detained docket population | 7.3 million | Feb. 26, 2026 |
| With final orders of removal | ~1.6 million | Feb. 26, 2026 |
| Individuals in ICE detention | 66,978 | Apr. 9, 2026 |
| Detention bedspace capacity | ~70,000 | April 2026 |
| Planned capacity | 90,000+ | FY2026 plans |
| Enrolled in Alternatives to Detention | 180,000 | April 2026 |

Source: Congressional Research Service, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Non-Detained Docket (NDD), IF13208, Apr. 24, 2026, https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/IF/PDF/IF13208/IF13208.1.pdf

Notes:
- The non-detained docket includes, per CRS: aliens released at ICE's discretion; aliens incarcerated in federal, state and local facilities while serving criminal sentences; those with final orders but withholding of removal or Convention Against Torture protection; those in the repatriation process; those whose countries do not cooperate with removal; fugitives with final orders; and erroneous entries (aliens who have died or departed voluntarily).
- The docket has more than tripled since FY2016, when it stood at 2.2 million. From FY1996 through FY2025 the average annual detained population ranged from roughly 9,000 to 60,000.
- The 425,431 convicted criminals counted in Table A1 (July 21, 2024) are a subset of the non-detained docket counted here.
- Supervision on the docket is minimal: per CRS, most non-detained docket aliens are not in ATD and typically must check in with ICE once a year.

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| Sept. 8, 2022 | Ibarra apprehended entering the United States illegally near El Paso; released pending his immigration case. |
| Aug. 31, 2023 | Arrested by New York City police on a child-endangerment charge; released before ICE could lodge a detainer. |

| Nov. 20, 2024 | Convicted on all 10 counts following a bench trial; sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. |

Notes:
- ICE confirmed Ibarra's illegal entry and prior New York arrest; ICE said he was released by New York authorities before a detainer could be issued.
- The brief cites this case, per the author's outline, as the sole illustrative victim case.

---

# Federal Data Show 13,099 Convicted Killers Outside ICE Custody: FSI Brief

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026 — The Founders' Square Institute today released Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Brett Kessler, senior fellow for immigration policy. The brief draws on the federal government's own records to document the public-safety cost of weak interior enforcement.

The core findings:

- ICE reported to Congress that as of July 21, 2024, 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions were on the agency's non-detained docket, none in ICE custody, including 13,099 convicted of homicide and 15,811 of sexual assault.
