# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14** | Founders' Square Institute
**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy** | Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- ICE reported to Congress that 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions were on its non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, none of them in ICE custody. They included 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault and 13,423 convicted of weapons offenses.
- The U.S. Sentencing Commission reports that noncitizens accounted for 44 percent of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2025 (28,886 of 66,662), 92 percent of them illegal aliens; in fiscal 2024 the share was 34.7 percent.
- Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem testified that sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 ICE detainers in 2025, and ICE records show 25,283 detainers declined from October 2022 through February 2025. Congress should fund criminal-alien detention, condition federal grants on detainer compliance, codify the 287(g) program and mandate public reporting on releases.

## 1. The non-detained docket

The clearest measure of what weak interior enforcement costs the public is the list ICE keeps of removable aliens it is not holding. In a September 2024 letter to Congress, ICE reported that as of July 21, 2024, its national docket carried 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories: 435,719 convicted criminals, plus another 226,847 with pending criminal charges. Of the convicted criminals, 425,431 were on the non-detained docket, which means not one of them was in ICE custody.

The convictions on that list are not minor. Grouped by ICE's most serious charge categories, the non-detained docket that day carried 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault, 62,231 convicted of assault, 13,423 convicted of weapons offenses and 56,533 convicted of dangerous-drug offenses. Every homicide conviction stands for a victim. On this list alone there are 13,099.

The docket also dwarfs the system built to contain it. The Congressional Research Service reports that the non-detained docket stood at 7.3 million aliens as of February 2026, more than triple its size in 2016, while ICE holds bedspace for roughly 70,000 detainees and had 66,978 people in custody on April 9, 2026. Detention capacity is the constant; the docket is the variable. Aliens on the non-detained docket are, in the typical case, subject to no supervision beyond an annual check-in with ICE.

The docket has victims. Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was murdered while jogging on the University of Georgia campus in Athens on Feb. 22, 2024. Her killer, Jose Ibarra, was a Venezuelan national who crossed the border illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and was released pending his immigration case. He was convicted on all 10 counts in November 2024 and sentenced to life without parole. Nothing about his path through the system was unusual. That is the point.

## 2. Federal sentencing

The federal courts tell the same story at the other end of the process. The U.S. Sentencing Commission reports that of the 66,662 individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2025, 28,886, or 44 percent, were not U.S. citizens. Nine in 10 of those noncitizens, 92 percent, were illegal aliens. A year earlier, noncitizens were 34.7 percent of everyone sentenced, 21,304 people, of whom 88.7 percent were illegal aliens.

The most common guideline under which noncitizens are sentenced is immigration: unlawful entry and unlawful reentry, offenses that by definition require illegal presence in the country. Drug trafficking is the second most common, at 17.6 percent of noncitizen sentences in fiscal 2024 and 12 percent in fiscal 2025.

These are federal numbers, and federal numbers are a floor. Most crime is prosecuted in state court, where the immigration status of defendants is generally not recorded at all. What the federal data establish is scale: in a single fiscal year, tens of thousands of illegal aliens were sentenced in federal court, and noncitizens were 44 percent of the entire federal sentencing docket.

## 3. What the Texas data show

Texas keeps the best state-level record of criminal-alien offending, because its Department of Public Safety records the immigration status of people booked into its jails and follows up as more of them are identified in prison. No other state keeps comparable records.

Read in full, the Texas data do not flatter illegal immigration. The Center for Immigration Studies, analyzing DPS conviction records, concludes that illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates than the general population for the most serious crimes, homicide and sexual assault included, once offenders identified as illegal immigrants only after incarceration are counted. The reason is straightforward: DPS does not learn every offender's immigration status at booking, and analyses that use only booking-stage identifications classify as native-born a significant number of offenders whom Texas later identifies as illegal immigrants. The undercount falls hardest on the most serious crimes, where sentences are longest and identification most often comes late.

That is a methodological dispute, but it is a dispute about how many victims illegal immigration produces, in the one state that keeps the records capable of answering it.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers

A detainer is ICE's request that a jail hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours after he would otherwise be released, so that ICE can take him into custody. Sanctuary policies instruct jails not to honor them, and the Department of Homeland Security is now counting the consequences. Testifying before the House Judiciary Committee on March 4, 2026, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem reported that sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 detainers in 2025. ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies show 25,283 detainers declined from fiscal 2023 through Feb. 6, 2025, a count that grew every year, and more than 1,400 instances in which a jail failed to give ICE adequate notice before releasing an alien. California's jails alone declined 13,025 detainers, 52 percent of the total.

Jose Ibarra passed through this door as well. New York police arrested him in August 2023 on a charge of endangering a child and released him before ICE could lodge a detainer, in a city that does not honor them. Months later, Laken Riley was dead.

A declined detainer is a decision, made by a public official, to release a removable criminal alien rather than transfer him to federal custody. The federal data show that officials made that decision more than 17,000 times last year.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund criminal-alien detention.** Appropriate what ICE needs to carry out its planned expansion beyond 90,000 beds in fiscal 2026, and direct that the added capacity be reserved first for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, including by taking custody as they complete criminal sentences.
2. **Condition federal grants on detainer compliance.** Make honoring ICE detainers and giving timely notice of release conditions of eligibility for Justice Department and DHS law-enforcement grants, and direct the attorney general to withhold funds from jurisdictions that decline.
3. **Codify and fund 287(g).** Write the 287(g) program into statute, beyond the reach of any future administration, and appropriate training funds for every willing law-enforcement agency. ICE now has 2,679 agreements in force; there is no reason the number cannot double.
4. **Require public reporting.** Direct DHS to publish quarterly, and by jurisdiction, the number of declined detainers, failed notifications and criminal aliens released from state and local custody, and to keep reporting the criminal composition of the non-detained docket.

Congress does not need new evidence. The federal government has been producing it for years, in letters, sentencing data and testimony. It needs to act on it.

*All figures are dated and sourced in the data appendix accompanying this brief.*

- Category figures count individuals whose most serious conviction falls in that category; individuals may have additional convictions.
- The letter responds to a March 13, 2024 request and reports docket data "as of July 21, 2024."

| Individuals sentenced, all | 61,678 | 66,662 |
| Non-U.S. citizens sentenced | 21,304 | 28,886 |

Notes:
- Fiscal years end Sept. 30. Federal sentences only; state prosecutions are excluded, and most crime is prosecuted in state court.
- Immigration offenses (unlawful entry, unlawful reentry) can be committed only by noncitizens, so the noncitizen share of the federal docket is driven largely by immigration prosecutions: 72.3 percent of noncitizen sentences in FY2024 and 79 percent in FY2025 were under the immigration guideline. Drug trafficking was second in both years.
- The noncitizen share of federal sentences fluctuates with prosecution priorities; it was 42.7 percent as far back as FY2018 (see Table A3). The brief reports FY2025 as the most recent full fiscal year and FY2024 as the prior-year comparison.

## Table A4. Texas DPS data: illegal-immigrant criminality, 2013-2022

| Item | Finding |
|---|---|
| Cato Institute analysis of Texas DPS data, 2013-2022 | Homicide conviction rate per 100,000: illegal immigrants 2.2; legal immigrants 1.2; native-born Americans 3.0. Illegal immigrants 26 percent less likely than native-born Americans to be convicted of homicide. |
| CIS critique of that analysis | Texas DPS identifies many illegal immigrants only after incarceration, so booking-stage analyses misclassify significant numbers as native-born; properly interpreted, the same DPS data show illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates than the general population for serious crimes including homicide and sexual assault. |

Sources: Alex Nowrasteh, Illegal Immigrant Murderers in Texas, 2013-2022: Illegal Immigrant and Legal Immigrant Conviction and Arrest Rates for Homicide and Other Crimes, Cato Institute Policy Analysis No. 977, Jun. 26, 2024, https://www.cato.org/policy-analysis/illegal-immigrant-murderers-texas-2013-2022; Sean Kennedy, Jason Richwine and Steven A. Camarota, Misuse of Texas Data Understates Illegal Immigrant Criminality, Center for Immigration Studies, Oct. 11, 2022, https://cis.org/Report/Misuse-Texas-Data-Understates-Illegal-Immigrant-Criminality

Notes (style sheet B3: counter-research in appendix only, one line, followed by CIS's methodological critique):
- The two organizations reach opposite conclusions from the same underlying DPS records. The dispute turns on the denominator: whether offenders identified as illegal immigrants only after incarceration are counted, and how illegal immigrants never identified by DPS are treated.
- Cato responds that CIS's alternative figures double-count offenders across DPS columns; CIS replies that DPS's "illegal" and "prison" columns do not overlap (J. Richwine, Continued Misuse of Texas Crime Data, Center for Immigration Studies, Oct. 20, 2022, https://cis.org/Richwine/Continued-Misuse-Texas-Crime-Data; A. Nowrasteh, The Center for Immigration Studies Is Still Wrong About Illegal Immigrant Crime in Texas, https://www.alexnowrasteh.com/p/the-center-for-immigration-studies; J. Richwine, Cato's Brazenly False Claim About Our Illegal Immigrant Crime Research, https://cis.org/Richwine/Catos-Brazenly-False-Claim-About-Our-Illegal-Immigrant-Crime-Research).
- Cato notes data-quality caveats for non-homicide offenses in DPS records. The brief's Section 3 attributes the higher-conviction reading to CIS.
- Texas is the only state that records criminal convictions and arrests by immigration status, per the Cato analysis and Nowrasteh's congressional testimony; DPS obtains the data through biometric checks with DHS and tracks arrestees through conviction.
- DPS reports separate counts for legal immigrants, illegal immigrants and a third category ("unknown or other") that Cato treats as native-born; treatment of that category is central to the denominator dispute above.

- Counts current as of Oct. 15, 2026, per ICE; agreements are added and terminated continuously.

# Federal Data Show 13,099 Convicted Killers Outside ICE Custody: FSI Brief

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026 — The Founders' Square Institute today released Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Brett Kessler, senior fellow for immigration policy. The brief draws on the federal government's own records to document the public-safety cost of weak interior enforcement.

The core findings:

- ICE reported to Congress that as of July 21, 2024, 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions were on the agency's non-detained docket, none in ICE custody, including 13,099 convicted of homicide and 15,811 of sexual assault.
- Noncitizens accounted for 44 percent of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2025, and 92 percent of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 ICE detainers in 2025, per Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem's March congressional testimony.

"Every number in this brief comes from the government's own records," Kessler said. "More than 425,000 convicted criminals sit on ICE's non-detained docket, nearly 13,100 of them killers, and sanctuary cities refused almost 18,000 detainers last year alone. These are policy choices, and Congress can reverse them."

The brief urges Congress to fund ICE's planned detention expansion beyond 90,000 beds and reserve that capacity for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket; to condition federal law-enforcement grants on honoring ICE detainers; to write the 287(g) program, now 2,679 agreements strong, into statute; and to require quarterly public reporting, by jurisdiction, of declined detainers and criminal-alien releases.

"Congress does not need new evidence. The federal government has been producing it for years," Kessler said. "It needs to act on it."

Brief No. 14, its data appendix and a Hill fact sheet are available from the FSI Office of Communications.

The Founders' Square Institute is a public-policy think tank in Washington, D.C.

---
